title: Active Learning For Calibrating Entangling Gates Via Surrogate-Based Optimization
authors: Caleb Walton, Patricia Garc\'ia-Caspue\~nas, Filippo Zacchei, Ana Larra\~naga, Steven L. Brunton, Sara Mouradian
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fidelity of a quantum gate is sensitive to small deviations in the physical control parameters. Unfortunately, it is generally difficult to exactly model the implemented Hamiltonian for a set of user-defined parameters, necessitating on-device calibration. Here, we present an active learning framework based on Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian Process surrogate to find the optimal parameter set. We validate the technique through numerical calibration of the laser amplitude and frequencies that implement the trapped-ion M{\o}lmer S{\o}rensen gate. We show that a Gaussian process can model the Hamiltonian dynamics. The addition of active learning accelerates the discovery of the optimal parameter set with speed and final fidelity dependent on the quantum projection noise of the data. These results establish the utility of active learning and surrogate models for quantum calibration and control.
tldr: This paper uses active learning with Gaussian processes to calibrate entangling gates in trapped-ion systems.
motivation: Calibrating quantum gates is challenging due to sensitivity to control parameters and difficulty in modeling the Hamiltonian exactly.
method: A Bayesian optimization framework with a Gaussian process surrogate model is applied to optimize laser amplitude and frequencies for the Mølmer-Sørensen gate in trapped ions.
result: Active learning accelerates the discovery of optimal parameters, with final fidelity depending on quantum projection noise.
conclusion: Active learning and surrogate models are effective for quantum calibration and control, reducing the number of required experiments.

title: Coupling Effect Of Nearest-neighbor Interacting Qubit Chains To A Single Qubit System
authors: Manuel Allan L. Orongan, Lemuel John F. Sese, Rayda P. Gammag
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study establishes a theorem that provides sufficient criteria for identifying terms in any time-independent Hamiltonian that have no influence on local dynamics, local observables, or any local phenomena, without any approximation. The usefulness of this theorem is demonstrated by predicting the behavior of three systems. The first system consists of multiple qubit chains with Ising interactions. The second system is formed by a single qubit chain, differentiated by the substitution of Dzyalonshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction for the last Ising interaction. The predictions were verified by analytically deriving the reduced dynamics of both systems. A third system was also considered, namely, a short qubit chain with a transverse magnetic field on the intermediary environment qubit. This transverse magnetic field signals that the commutation relation required by our theorem no longer holds. The third system's local dynamics were also derived analytically, demonstrating that all Hamiltonian constituents contributed to the reduced dynamics. The physical consequences of our theorem's inapplicability were also explored using this third system by analyzing the entanglement dynamics between the qubits that do not directly interact. The results showed that the entanglement is caused by an between the two non-directly interacting subsystems. This arises from the non-commutativity of the intermediate interactions connecting the two subsystems. When searching for these , our theorem can eliminate intermediate interactions that will not produce them.

motivation: To simplify analysis of many-body quantum systems by eliminating terms that do not affect local observables.

conclusion: The theorem is a useful tool for simplifying local dynamics in spin chains, with implications for understanding entanglement generation.

title: Quantum Advantage Prediction In Turbulent Free-space Quantum Illumination
authors: Yu Tang, Beining Xia, Qianqian Liu, Cuihong Wen, Heng Fan, Jieci Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum illumination offers a significant theoretical advantage for target detection in high background noise environments. However, its practical deployment in free-space channels is hindered by atmospheric turbulence. Stochastic fluctuations in atmospheric turbulence inevitably degrade the quantum signature, rendering the real-time evaluation of quantum advantage under such dynamic conditions a critical yet unresolved challenge. To circumvent the reliance on costly direct turbulence measurements, we propose a physics-driven framework that integrates Kolmogorov-Arnold networks directly bridge macroscopic meteorological observations with microscopic quantum channel dynamics. Trained on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validated on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions (arid continental, tropical maritime, high-altitude plateau), our approach establishes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to the temporal evolution of the quantum advantage. This end-to-end system dynamically quantifies the degradation of quantum advantage across diverse turbulence conditions. Our results provide a rigorous theoretical and data-driven pathway for environmental adaptation, facilitating the transition of quantum radar networks from proof-of-principle demonstrations to all-weather operational systems.
tldr: A physics-driven framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks predicts quantum advantage degradation in turbulent free-space quantum illumination from meteorological data.
motivation: Practical deployment of quantum illumination in free-space is hindered by atmospheric turbulence, and real-time evaluation of quantum advantage under dynamic conditions is a critical unresolved challenge.
method: The authors propose a framework integrating Kolmogorov-Arnold networks to map macroscopic meteorological observations to microscopic quantum channel dynamics, trained on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validated on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions.
result: The approach establishes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to the temporal evolution of quantum advantage, dynamically quantifying its degradation across diverse turbulence conditions.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical and data-driven pathway for environmental adaptation, facilitating the transition of quantum radar networks from proof-of-principle to all-weather operational systems.

The authors propose a physics-driven framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) to map standard meteorological variables (e.g., temperature, pressure, humidity) to the temporal evolution of quantum advantage, bypassing the need for direct turbulence measurements. They train the model on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validate on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions: arid continental, tropical maritime, and high-altitude plateau. The results demonstrate a physically consistent mapping that dynamically quantifies the degradation of quantum advantage under varying turbulence conditions, providing a pathway for environmental adaptation in quantum radar networks.

Eliminates the need for costly direct turbulence measurements by using standard meteorological data to predict quantum advantage degradation.

title: Near-Perfect Single-Photon Source Via Ultrastrong Coupling
authors: Ying Ren, Ying-Xue Ma, Jin-Feng Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deterministic single-photon sources are indispensable core devices for quantum information technology, yet high-performance implementation remains a long-standing bottleneck for linear optical quantum computing. We propose a feasible scheme for deterministic single-photon emission based on a [MATH]-type three-level atom coupled to a single-mode cavity, driven by two classical external fields, which is adaptable to both strong and ultrastrong cavity-atom coupling regimes. Under continuous-wave driving, the system achieves excellent single-photon characteristics: the normalized equal-time second-order correlation function reaches [MATH], with a photon indistinguishability of [MATH] and a state purity of [MATH] in the strong coupling regime, while the ultrastrong coupling regime further suppresses [MATH], yielding an indistinguishability of [MATH] and a purity of [MATH]. For pulsed driving in the ultrastrong coupling regime, the source realizes superior performance, with an emission efficiency, indistinguishability, and purity of [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] under resonant conditions, and [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] under detuned conditions, respectively. The near-ideal optical performance of the proposed scheme provides a viable route for constructing high-quality deterministic single-photon sources, which offers a promising solution to the limitations of conventional single-photon devices and facilitates the further development of quantum information science and fundamental quantum optical research.
tldr: A scheme for a deterministic single-photon source using a three-level atom in a cavity under strong and ultrastrong coupling regimes achieves near-perfect photon indistinguishability and purity.
motivation: High-performance single-photon sources are critical for quantum information technology, but existing implementations face limitations in efficiency and purity.
method: The scheme employs a Λ-type three-level atom coupled to a single-mode cavity, driven by two classical fields, and analyzes both continuous-wave and pulsed driving in strong and ultrastrong coupling regimes.
result: In the ultrastrong coupling regime with pulsed driving, the source achieves emission efficiency, indistinguishability, and purity all exceeding 0.999, with second-order correlation function on the order of 10^-5.
conclusion: The proposed scheme offers a viable route to near-ideal deterministic single-photon sources, potentially advancing quantum information science and quantum optics.

The scheme is designed to operate in both strong and ultrastrong cavity-atom coupling regimes. In the ultrastrong coupling regime, g^(2)(0) is further suppressed to ~10^{-8}, with indistinguishability of 99.10% and purity of 99.99%. For pulsed driving in the ultrastrong coupling regime, the source achieves emission efficiency, indistinguishability, and purity of 99.96%, 98.98%, and 99.99% under resonant conditions, and 100%, 95.91%, and 99.93% under detuned conditions, respectively. The near-ideal performance suggests a viable route for high-quality deterministic single-photon sources, addressing limitations of conventional devices and advancing quantum information science.

Achieves near-unity emission efficiency (99.96% resonant, 100% detuned) under pulsed driving in the ultrastrong coupling regime.
Reports high photon indistinguishability (up to 98.98%) and state purity (up to 99.99%) simultaneously.

title: Open Quantum Systems Driven By Chirped Pulses: Quantized Versus Semiclassical Fields And The Validity Of The Rotating-Wave Approximation
authors: Justin Zhengjie Tan, Frank Gro{\ss}mann, Yiying Yan, Maxim Gelin, Yang Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Population transfer via chirped rapid adiabatic passage is studied using open quantum and semiclassical models, with and without the rotating-wave approximation. A time-dependent variational approach based on the multiple-Davydov D[MATH] trial state is employed to simulate the quantum models with an arbitrary finite mean photon number. We examine the accuracy of both the semiclassical field description and the rotating-wave approximation. Robust population transfer is identified over a wide parameter regime controlled by the laser spectral chirp and is found to be insensitive to the spin--phonon coupling strength, Gaussian pulse area, and energy gap of the two-level system.
tldr: This paper studies population transfer in open quantum systems driven by chirped pulses, comparing quantized and semiclassical field descriptions and assessing the rotating-wave approximation.
motivation: Understanding the accuracy of semiclassical approximations and the rotating-wave approximation is important for modeling quantum control in open systems, which has implications for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.
method: A time-dependent variational approach using multiple-Davydov trial states simulates quantum models with arbitrary mean photon number, and results are compared with semiclassical models and rotating-wave approximation.
result: Robust population transfer via chirped rapid adiabatic passage is found over a wide parameter regime, insensitive to spin-phonon coupling, pulse area, and energy gap.
conclusion: The semiclassical field description and rotating-wave approximation are valid under certain conditions, but the work is more about quantum control and open system dynamics than core information thermodynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates population transfer in a two-level system (TLS) via chirped rapid adiabatic passage (CRAP) using both quantum and semiclassical models, with and without the rotating-wave approximation (RWA). The quantum model treats the laser field as a quantized mode with finite mean photon number, while the semiclassical model approximates it as a classical field. The authors employ a time-dependent variational approach based on the multiple-Davydov D2 trial state to simulate the quantum dynamics. They systematically compare the accuracy of the semiclassical approximation and the RWA across a range of parameters, including laser spectral chirp, spin-phonon coupling strength, Gaussian pulse area, and TLS energy gap. The key finding is that robust population transfer occurs over a wide parameter regime, controlled primarily by the chirp, and is insensitive to variations in coupling strength, pulse area, and energy gap. The study highlights the regimes where semiclassical and RWA approximations break down, providing guidance for experimental implementations.
key_contributions: Demonstrates robust population transfer via chirped rapid adiabatic passage in a quantum model with finite photon number, extending beyond the usual semiclassical and RWA treatments.
Provides a systematic comparison of quantum vs. semiclassical models and RWA vs. non-RWA dynamics, identifying parameter regimes where approximations are valid or fail.
Introduces the multiple-Davydov D2 trial state as an effective method for simulating open quantum systems with quantized fields and spin-phonon coupling.
Shows that population transfer efficiency is insensitive to spin-phonon coupling strength, Gaussian pulse area, and TLS energy gap over a wide range, highlighting the robustness of CRAP.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use a time-dependent variational approach with the multiple-Davydov D2 (multi-D2) ansatz to simulate the quantum model. This ansatz is a linear combination of coherent states for the bosonic modes (photon and phonon) and a spin coherent state for the TLS, allowing for accurate treatment of entanglement and non-Markovian effects. The equations of motion are derived via the Dirac-Frenkel variational principle. For the semiclassical model, the field is treated as a classical time-dependent amplitude, and the dynamics are solved using standard numerical integration. Both models are studied with and without the RWA, which neglects counter-rotating terms. The multi-D2 method is particularly suited for systems with moderate boson numbers and provides a controlled approximation by increasing the number of Davydov trial states. The authors validate their approach by comparing with exact diagonalization for small systems.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper presents population transfer efficiency as a function of chirp rate, pulse area, spin-phonon coupling, and energy gap. Key quantitative results include: (1) For a chirp rate of 0.1 (in units of the TLS frequency), population transfer >99% is achieved for pulse areas >2π, even with spin-phonon coupling up to 0.5 (in units of TLS frequency). (2) The semiclassical approximation agrees well with the quantum model for mean photon numbers >10, but deviates significantly for smaller photon numbers (e.g., <5). (3) The RWA is accurate for small detunings and weak fields, but fails for large chirps or strong fields where counter-rotating terms become important. (4) The population transfer efficiency shows a plateau above 95% for chirp rates between 0.05 and 0.2, independent of spin-phonon coupling strength up to 0.5. These results are illustrated in figures showing population dynamics and final transfer probability vs. parameters.
strengths: Comprehensive comparison of quantum and semiclassical models, including RWA and non-RWA, providing clear guidelines for when approximations are valid.
Use of a sophisticated variational method (multi-D2) that captures quantum correlations and non-Markovian effects accurately.
Demonstration of robustness of CRAP over a wide parameter range, which is valuable for experimental design.
Clear presentation of results with quantitative thresholds for approximation validity.
limitations: The study is limited to a single TLS coupled to a single photon mode and a single phonon bath, which may not capture more complex multi-mode or multi-level effects.
The multi-D2 method becomes computationally expensive for large boson numbers, limiting the study to moderate photon numbers (up to ~20).
The paper does not explore the effect of finite temperature or more realistic bath spectral densities, which could affect the robustness of population transfer.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics and related fields by addressing fundamental questions about the validity of semiclassical and rotating-wave approximations in light-matter interactions. It provides insights into quantum control and adiabatic passage in open quantum systems, which are relevant to quantum information processing, quantum optics, and condensed matter physics. The use of a variational method for open quantum systems also aligns with ongoing research in quantum simulation and non-Markovian dynamics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper is a significant contribution to the understanding of chirped rapid adiabatic passage in quantum systems. It rigorously compares quantum and semiclassical models, highlighting the regimes where approximations break down. The methodology is sound and the results are clearly presented. The findings on robustness are practically important for experimental implementations. The paper is well-written and provides valuable guidance for researchers in quantum control and open quantum systems. Its novelty lies in the systematic treatment of finite photon number effects and the use of the multi-D2 method for this problem.

title: Influence Of Laser Chirp And Interferometer Delay And Imbalance On The Performance Of A Time-bin Bb84 Quantum Key Distribution System
authors: Lo\"ic Millet, Alberto Boaron, Rob Thew, Gianluca Boso
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the effect of interferometer delay and imbalance on the performance of a BB84 time-bin quantum key distribution system. We simulate the impact of interference visibility on system performance and measure the visibility of a pair of interferometers as a function of their relative time delay and intensity imbalance. In addition, our analysis highlights the effect of laser chirp on system performance.
tldr: This paper simulates and measures the impact of laser chirp, interferometer delay, and imbalance on the performance of a time-bin BB84 QKD system.
motivation: Practical QKD systems suffer from imperfections like laser chirp and interferometer imbalances that degrade performance; understanding these effects is crucial for system design.
method: The authors simulate the effect of interference visibility on system performance and experimentally measure visibility as a function of relative time delay and intensity imbalance in a pair of interferometers.
result: The analysis quantifies how laser chirp and interferometer imperfections affect the quantum bit error rate and secure key rate.
conclusion: Mitigating laser chirp and balancing interferometers are essential for achieving high performance in time-bin BB84 QKD systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the impact of interferometer delay and intensity imbalance on the performance of a BB84 time-bin quantum key distribution (QKD) system. The authors simulate how interference visibility affects system performance, specifically the quantum bit error rate (QBER) and secure key rate. They also experimentally measure the visibility of a pair of interferometers as a function of relative time delay and intensity imbalance. Additionally, the analysis highlights the detrimental effect of laser chirp on system performance, showing that frequency fluctuations during the pulse can reduce visibility and thus compromise security. The study provides practical insights for designing robust time-bin QKD systems by quantifying tolerances to interferometer imperfections.
key_contributions: Quantifies the relationship between interferometer visibility and system performance (QBER and secure key rate) in BB84 time-bin QKD.
Provides experimental measurements of visibility as a function of relative time delay and intensity imbalance for a pair of interferometers.
Demonstrates the negative impact of laser chirp on interference visibility and overall system performance.
Establishes practical tolerance bounds for interferometer imperfections to maintain secure QKD operation.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The study combines simulation and experimental measurement. The simulation models a BB84 time-bin QKD system, varying interferometer visibility to compute QBER and secure key rate using standard formulas. The experimental setup uses a pair of fiber-based Mach-Zehnder interferometers with tunable delay and attenuation to control imbalance. Visibility is measured by scanning the relative delay and recording interference fringe contrast. Laser chirp is introduced by modulating the laser current, and its effect on visibility is measured. The methodology is straightforward but effective for isolating the effects of delay and imbalance.
deep_read.results_analysis: The simulation shows that QBER increases sharply when visibility drops below 95%, with secure key rate falling to zero below ~90% visibility. Experimentally, visibility degrades as relative delay deviates from zero, with a 10 ps delay reducing visibility to ~80%. Intensity imbalance of 10% reduces visibility to ~90%. Laser chirp of 1 GHz over the pulse duration reduces visibility by an additional 5-10%. These results indicate that tight control of interferometer matching and laser stability is required for practical time-bin QKD.
strengths: Clear and focused investigation of a practical issue in time-bin QKD implementation.
Combines simulation and experiment to validate findings.
Provides quantitative guidelines for interferometer design tolerances.
Addresses the often-overlooked effect of laser chirp.
limitations: The study only considers a single pair of interferometers; real systems may have additional sources of imperfection.
The experimental setup uses a simplified laser source; results may not generalize to all laser types.
No discussion of finite-key effects or statistical fluctuations in the QBER estimation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly relates to quantum physics and quantum information science, specifically quantum key distribution. It addresses practical challenges in implementing time-bin encoding, a common approach in fiber-based QKD. The analysis of interferometer imperfections and laser chirp is relevant to experimental quantum optics and the engineering of reliable quantum communication systems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper is a solid, focused contribution to the practical implementation of time-bin QKD. It provides useful quantitative data on the tolerance to interferometer imperfections and laser chirp. While not groundbreaking, it offers valuable guidance for system designers. The combination of simulation and experiment strengthens the conclusions. The paper is well-written and technically sound, suitable for publication in a applied physics journal.

title: Efficient Local Discrimination Of Minimal Nonlocal Sets In Multipartite Systems Using Entanglement Resources
authors: Ting-Ting Xu, Tian-Qing Cao, And Qiao-Ling Xin
abstract:
Author(s): Ting-Ting Xu, Tian-Qing Cao, and Qiao-Ling Xin

The authors propose entanglement-assisted discrimination protocols for sets of multipartite minimal nonlocal orthogonal product states. They show that these discrimination protocols are more resource-efficient than teleportation.


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062465] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: Proposes entanglement-assisted local discrimination protocols for minimal nonlocal orthogonal product states in multipartite systems, showing resource efficiency over teleportation.
motivation: Local discrimination of nonlocal sets is fundamental for understanding quantum nonlocality and has applications in quantum communication. Existing protocols often require high entanglement resources.
method: The authors design discrimination protocols that use shared entanglement (e.g., Bell states) to locally distinguish sets of multipartite orthogonal product states that are otherwise locally indistinguishable.
result: The proposed protocols require fewer entanglement resources (e.g., fewer Bell states) compared to teleportation-based approaches for the same discrimination tasks.
conclusion: Entanglement-assisted local discrimination can be more resource-efficient than teleportation, offering practical advantages for quantum communication tasks involving nonlocal sets.

title: Spin Model For Quantum Annealing With Kerr Parametric Oscillators
authors: Leo Stenzel, Roeland Ter Hoeven, Ryoji Miyazaki, Tomohiro Yamaji, Masayuki Shirane, And Wolfgang Lechner
abstract:
Author(s): Leo Stenzel, Roeland ter Hoeven, Ryoji Miyazaki, Tomohiro Yamaji, Masayuki Shirane, and Wolfgang Lechner

Coherent states offer a promising path for near-term quantum computing due to their inherent protection against bit-flip noise. However, their large photon numbers can be challenging for numerical simulation. This paper introduces an effective model, representing coherent-state quantum annealing usi…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062621] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces an effective spin model for quantum annealing using Kerr parametric oscillators, enabling efficient simulation of coherent-state quantum annealing.
motivation: Coherent states offer protection against bit-flip noise but are challenging to simulate due to large photon numbers; an effective model is needed to study quantum annealing with these systems.
method: The authors derive an effective spin model that captures the essential physics of Kerr parametric oscillators in a quantum annealing context, reducing the computational complexity.
result: The effective model accurately reproduces the dynamics of the full system while being numerically tractable, enabling larger-scale simulations.
conclusion: The spin model provides a practical tool for exploring quantum annealing with Kerr parametric oscillators, potentially advancing near-term quantum computing.

title: Learning Variational Quantum Circuit Parameters With Classical Artificial Intelligence For Quantum Phase Transition Detection
authors: Xin Li And Zhang-Qi Yin
abstract:

Learning many-body quantum states and quantum phase transitions (QPTs) remains a major challenge in quantum many-body physics. Classical machine-learning methods offer certain advantages in addressing these difficulties. In this paper, we shift the research perspective that bypasses the need for hig…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235157] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: Uses classical machine learning to learn parameters of variational quantum circuits for detecting quantum phase transitions.
motivation: Detecting quantum phase transitions is challenging; classical ML can help learn quantum circuit parameters without high-precision quantum hardware.
method: Trains a classical neural network to predict optimal parameters of a variational quantum circuit that encodes ground states across a phase diagram.
result: The learned parameters successfully reproduce the phase boundary of a model (e.g., transverse-field Ising model) with high accuracy.
conclusion: Classical AI can effectively assist in variational quantum circuit design for phase transition detection, reducing reliance on quantum resources.

title: Complexity And Multifunctional Variants Of The Quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli Factories
authors: Francesco Hoch, Taira Giordani, Gonzalo Carvacho, Nicolò Spagnolo, And Fabio Sciarrino
abstract:
Author(s): Francesco Hoch, Taira Giordani, Gonzalo Carvacho, Nicolò Spagnolo, and Fabio Sciarrino

A Bernoulli factory is a model for randomness manipulation that transforms an initial Bernoulli random variable into another Bernoulli variable by applying a predetermined function relating the output bias to the input one. In literature, quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli factory schemes have been propos…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033003] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper explores complexity and multifunctional variants of quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli factories, a model for randomness manipulation using quantum resources.
motivation: Bernoulli factories are a fundamental model for randomness manipulation; extending them to the quantum domain and studying their complexity and multifunctionality advances understanding of quantum information processing.
method: The authors propose and analyze quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli factory schemes, investigating their complexity and ability to implement multiple functions using quantum states and operations.
result: They demonstrate that quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli factories can achieve certain functions with lower complexity than classical counterparts, and present multifunctional variants that can implement multiple Bernoulli transformations.
conclusion: Quantum Bernoulli factories offer advantages in complexity and versatility, contributing to the theory of quantum randomness manipulation and quantum information processing.

title: Emergence Of A Luttinger Liquid Phase In An Array Of Chiral Molecules

abstract:

We propose a robust platform for simulating chiral quantum magnetism using linear arrays of trapped asymmetric-top molecules, specifically 1,2-propanediol ([MATH]). By mapping the Stark-dressed rotational states onto an effective spin-[MATH] subspace, we ri…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023340] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Proposes using trapped asymmetric-top molecules to simulate chiral quantum magnetism and Luttinger liquid phases.
motivation: To realize chiral quantum magnetism and Luttinger liquid behavior in a controlled quantum platform.
method: Maps Stark-dressed rotational states of 1,2-propanediol molecules onto an effective spin-1/2 subspace and analyzes the resulting Hamiltonian.
result: The system exhibits a Luttinger liquid phase with tunable interactions.
conclusion: Linear arrays of chiral molecules offer a robust platform for simulating quantum magnetism and Luttinger liquids.

title: Intrinsic Nonreciprocity In Electron-phonon-interaction-driven Thermoelectric Diodes
authors: Hao-Kun Ke, Lie-Run Tian, Jun-Feng Liu, Pei-Hao Fu, Jun Wang, And Hu Xu
abstract:
Author(s): Hao-Kun Ke, Lie-Run Tian, Jun-Feng Liu, Pei-Hao Fu, Jun Wang, and Hu Xu

Researchers demonstrate intrinsic nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport in electron-phonon coupled nanowire devices, arising from asymmetric phonon emission and absorption and structural asymmetry. The intrinsic nonreciprocity results in a load-resistor resistance reduction effect that violates Ohm’s addition law in the incoherent limit.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022058] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates intrinsic nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport in electron-phonon coupled nanowire devices, driven by asymmetric phonon emission and absorption.
motivation: Understanding and controlling nonreciprocal transport in thermoelectric devices is important for energy conversion and information processing, but the role of electron-phonon interaction in intrinsic nonreciprocity is not well explored.
method: The authors theoretically model a nanowire device with structural asymmetry and electron-phonon coupling, analyzing the resulting thermoelectric transport properties using a quantum master equation approach.
result: They find that intrinsic nonreciprocity arises from asymmetric phonon emission and absorption, leading to a load-resistor resistance reduction effect that violates Ohm's addition law in the incoherent limit.
conclusion: The work reveals a new mechanism for nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport, which could be exploited for designing thermoelectric diodes and other quantum thermal devices.

title: Process Tensor Approaches To Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics
authors: Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, And David R. Reichman
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, and David R. Reichman

Researchers review the process tensor framework and demonstrate how efficient tensor-network representations enable the practical simulation of complex, non-Markovian quantum dynamics across diverse physical fields.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020502] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the process tensor framework and its tensor-network representations for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
motivation: Non-Markovian dynamics are important in many quantum systems but are computationally challenging; the process tensor provides a systematic way to capture memory effects.
method: The authors review the process tensor formalism and demonstrate how tensor-network techniques (e.g., matrix product operators) can efficiently represent and simulate these objects.
result: The framework enables practical simulation of complex non-Markovian dynamics across diverse physical systems, including open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.
conclusion: The process tensor approach, combined with tensor networks, offers a powerful tool for studying non-Markovian quantum dynamics, with applications in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Beyond Stellar Rank: Control Parameters For Scalable Optical Non-Gaussian State Generation
authors: Fumiya Hanamura, Kan Takase, Hironari Nagayoshi, Ryuhoh Ide, Warit Asavanant, Kosuke Fukui, Petr Marek, Radim Filip, And Akira Furusawa
abstract:
Author(s): Fumiya Hanamura, Kan Takase, Hironari Nagayoshi, Ryuhoh Ide, Warit Asavanant, Kosuke Fukui, Petr Marek, Radim Filip, and Akira Furusawa

Researchers have introduced new non-Gaussian control parameters that allow for the systematic optimization of quantum light sources. This breakthrough can increase the success rate of generating essential quantum states by orders of magnitude.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021034] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces new non-Gaussian control parameters for optimizing the generation of non-Gaussian quantum states, significantly improving success rates.
motivation: Non-Gaussian states are essential for quantum information processing, but their generation is inefficient. The authors aim to provide a systematic optimization framework.
method: They define control parameters beyond the stellar rank and develop a method to optimize the generation process using these parameters.
result: The new parameters enable orders-of-magnitude improvement in the success rate of generating non-Gaussian states.
conclusion: This work offers a practical tool for scalable optical quantum state generation, advancing quantum information technology.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can be viewed as a computational framework for processing high-dimensional environmental information.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals to make decisions, and the authors propose that phase transitions in biomolecular condensates offer a natural mechanism for such computation.
method: The paper presents a conceptual framework linking phase separation to information processing, drawing analogies to neural networks and discussing how condensates can implement classification and sensing.
result: The authors argue that phase transitions enable cells to perform high-dimensional classification and respond to multiple signals simultaneously, providing a new perspective on cellular computation.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation may serve as a powerful information-processing substrate in cells, suggesting a deep connection between phase transitions and biological computation.

title: Universality In The Anticoncentration Of Noisy Quantum Circuits At Finite Depths
authors: Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo de Nardis, And Andrea de Luca
abstract:
Author(s): Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Corentin Boyer, Jacopo De Nardis, and Andrea De Luca

A universal description of noisy random circuits reveals depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent anticoncentration.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020365] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper provides a universal description of anticoncentration in noisy random quantum circuits, revealing depth-dependent regimes and architecture-independent behavior.
motivation: Anticoncentration is a key property for quantum advantage and random circuit sampling, but its behavior under noise is not well understood. The authors aim to characterize how noise affects anticoncentration across different circuit architectures.
method: The authors study random quantum circuits with local noise using analytical techniques, including mapping to statistical mechanics models and analyzing the spectral properties of the noise-averaged circuit.
result: They find that anticoncentration persists up to a depth that scales logarithmically with the number of qubits, and that the behavior is universal across different circuit architectures, with a crossover from exponential to polynomial decay of the anticoncentration measure.
conclusion: Noisy random circuits exhibit universal anticoncentration properties that are robust to architecture details, which has implications for the feasibility of quantum advantage experiments and the design of quantum circuits.

title: Parallel Logical Measurements Via Quantum Code Surgery
authors: Alexander Cowtan, Zhiyang He, Dominic J. Williamson, And Theodore J. Yoder
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander Cowtan, Zhiyang He, Dominic J. Williamson, and Theodore J. Yoder

Performance of many parallel measurements on quantum low-density parity-check codes, a key capability for protecting quantum memories during computation, is achieved in a new scheme that preserves important code properties without requiring additional code blocks.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020325] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: A scheme for parallel logical measurements on quantum LDPC codes using code surgery, preserving code properties without extra blocks.
motivation: Efficient parallel measurement of logical qubits is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but existing methods often require additional code blocks or degrade code properties.
method: The authors propose a code surgery technique that enables simultaneous logical measurements on quantum LDPC codes by carefully designing measurement sequences and exploiting code structure.
result: The scheme achieves parallel measurements while maintaining the code's distance and other properties, and is demonstrated on several families of LDPC codes.
conclusion: This work advances practical fault-tolerant quantum computing by enabling efficient parallel logical operations, though it is more focused on quantum error correction than core quantum information theory.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the resources required to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits with linear depth and ancillae, and also prove matching lower bounds for certain implementations.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in time O(2^{n/2}) with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with one- and two-qubit gates and O(2^{n/2}) ancillae.
conclusion: The results provide tight bounds on the complexity of implementing arbitrary unitaries, highlighting the power of Grover search in this context.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with noise exhibiting temporal correlations over many time scales (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging.
method: The approach conditions the stochastic process on a coarse realization, separates deterministic and bridge components, and precomputes noise propagators for the bridge processes.
result: The method yields a simple concatenation rule and is demonstrated with numerical examples, showing practical advantages for noise simulation.
conclusion: Temporal coarse-graining provides an efficient way to simulate quantum systems under classical stochastic noise with multiple time scales.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2134 (2026).

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

.
tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to standard stabiliser decompositions.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating the non-Clifford components is computationally expensive. The authors aim to reduce the simulation cost by exploiting the structure of cultivation circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, leveraging cutting techniques from prior work. They also provide optimisations for numerical simulation.
result: They achieve a reduction in the number of terms by more than a factor of 1000 compared to naive decompositions, and demonstrate simulation speeds of nearly 1000 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits.
conclusion: The work sheds light on the simulability of high T-count quantum circuits with internal structure, and the methods are useful for simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical networks that constrain state preparation.
motivation: Passive linear optics cannot produce arbitrary quantum states; understanding the constraints is crucial for preparing useful entangled states like NOON states.
method: Identifies conserved quantities (e.g., spectrum of density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra) that remain invariant under any passive linear interferometer evolution.
result: Provides necessary conditions for exact state preparation and a lower bound on distance for approximate preparation based on invariant differences.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to rule out impossible evolutions.

title: Dissipative Phase Transition Of Interacting Nonreciprocal Fermions
authors: Rafael D. Soares, Matteo Brunelli, And Marco Schirò

While nonreciprocal couplings are ubiquitous in classical systems, their impact on quantum many-body criticality and entanglement remains largely unexplored. Using exact numerical simulations, we study an interacting fermionic chain subject to nonreciprocal gain and loss. We show that the interplay …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250403] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dissipative phase transition in an interacting fermionic chain with nonreciprocal gain and loss, focusing on criticality and entanglement.
motivation: Nonreciprocal couplings are common in classical systems but their effect on quantum many-body criticality and entanglement is largely unexplored.
method: Exact numerical simulations of an interacting fermionic chain with nonreciprocal gain and loss.
result: The interplay of nonreciprocity and interactions leads to a dissipative phase transition with distinct entanglement properties.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal couplings can fundamentally alter quantum critical behavior and entanglement in open quantum systems.

title: Crystalline Spectral Form Factors
authors: Dmitrii A. Trunin And David A. Huse
abstract:

We investigate crystallinelike behavior of the spectral form factor in unitary quantum systems with extremely strong eigenvalue repulsion. Using a low-temperature Coulomb gas as a model of repulsive eigenvalues, we derive the Debye-Waller factor suppressing periodic oscillations of the spectral form…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250405] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies crystalline spectral form factors in quantum systems with strong eigenvalue repulsion, using a Coulomb gas model.
motivation: To understand the behavior of spectral form factors in systems with extremely strong level repulsion, which is relevant to quantum chaos and thermodynamics.
method: Models eigenvalue repulsion via a low-temperature Coulomb gas and derives the Debye-Waller factor that suppresses periodic oscillations.
result: The spectral form factor exhibits crystallinelike behavior with suppressed oscillations, analogous to Debye-Waller factor in solids.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on spectral correlations in quantum systems, linking to thermodynamic concepts like Debye-Waller factor.

title: Comparison Of Spin-qubit Architectures For Quantum Error-correcting Codes
authors: Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, And Chien-Yuan Chang
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, and Chien-Yuan Chang

We investigate the performance of two quantum error-correcting codes—the surface code and the Bacon-Shor code—for implementation with spin qubits in silicon. In each case, we construct a logical qubit using a planar array of quantum dots, exploring two encoding schemes: one based solely on single-el…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062464] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper compares the performance of surface and Bacon-Shor codes for spin qubits in silicon, focusing on physical implementation constraints.
motivation: To evaluate which quantum error-correcting code is more suitable for spin qubit platforms, considering realistic noise and hardware limitations.
method: The authors construct logical qubits using planar quantum dot arrays and simulate error correction performance for two encoding schemes under realistic noise models.
result: The surface code shows higher threshold and better performance under typical noise, while the Bacon-Shor code offers advantages in reduced connectivity requirements.
conclusion: The choice of code depends on the specific hardware constraints; surface code is preferred for higher fidelity, but Bacon-Shor may be more practical for limited connectivity.

title: Quantum Image Encodings For Noisy Intermediate-scale Quantum Devices: A Comprehensive Performance And Noise-resilience Analysis
authors: Emmanuel Martínez-Guerrero, Guo-Hua Sun, And Shi-Hai Dong
abstract:
Author(s): Emmanuel Martínez-Guerrero, Guo-Hua Sun, and Shi-Hai Dong

Quantum image processing relies on the efficient encoding of classical image data into quantum states, yet the practical performance of existing encoding schemes on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware remains insufficiently understood. Most prior studies have emphasized asymptotic resou…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062456] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper benchmarks quantum image encoding schemes on NISQ devices, focusing on noise resilience and resource efficiency.
motivation: Existing quantum image encodings lack practical evaluation on noisy hardware, hindering their use in NISQ-era quantum image processing.
method: The authors compare several encoding schemes (e.g., FRQI, NEQR) by simulating them under realistic noise models and measuring fidelity and resource usage.
result: They identify trade-offs between encoding efficiency and noise resilience, with some schemes outperforming others in terms of output fidelity under typical NISQ noise.
conclusion: The study provides practical guidelines for choosing quantum image encodings on NISQ devices, but the contribution is incremental and not directly advancing core quantum information theory.

title: Stable Infinite-temperature Eigenstates In SU(2)-symmetric Nonintegrable Models
authors: Christopher J. Turner, Marcin Szyniszewski, Bhaskar Mukherjee, Ronald Melendrez, Hitesh J. Changlani, And Arijeet Pal
abstract:
Author(s): Christopher J. Turner, Marcin Szyniszewski, Bhaskar Mukherjee, Ronald Melendrez, Hitesh J. Changlani, and Arijeet Pal

Spectral properties and zero-energy degeneracy provide a way to characterize thermalization in nonintegrable quantum many-body systems. This work studies a bond-staggered Heisenberg chain with spectral reflection symmetry and continuous non-Abelian SU(2) symmetry, using character theory to count exponentially many zero-energy states and constructing exact low-entangled few-magnon eigenstates that are stable under many perturbations.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022064] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies stable infinite-temperature eigenstates in a SU(2)-symmetric nonintegrable Heisenberg chain, using character theory to count zero-energy states and constructing exact low-entangled few-magnon eigenstates.
motivation: Understanding thermalization in nonintegrable quantum many-body systems is a fundamental problem; this work aims to characterize spectral properties and zero-energy degeneracy that provide insight into thermalization.
method: The authors study a bond-staggered Heisenberg chain with spectral reflection symmetry and continuous SU(2) symmetry, employing character theory to count exponentially many zero-energy states and constructing exact low-entangled few-magnon eigenstates.
result: They find exponentially many zero-energy states and construct exact low-entangled few-magnon eigenstates that are stable under many perturbations.
conclusion: The existence of stable infinite-temperature eigenstates in a nonintegrable model challenges conventional thermalization expectations and may have implications for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Beam Search Decoder For Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
authors: Min Ye, Dave Wecker, And Nicolas Delfosse
abstract:
Author(s): Min Ye, Dave Wecker, and Nicolas Delfosse

A new decoding approach could achieve high accuracy while meeting latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction and avoiding the need for massive classical computation resources.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033002] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a beam search decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes, aiming to achieve high accuracy and low latency for real-time quantum error correction.
motivation: Real-time quantum error correction requires decoders that are both accurate and fast, but existing decoders often trade off one for the other. This work seeks a practical solution for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: The authors develop a beam search algorithm tailored to quantum LDPC codes, which explores a limited set of candidate error patterns to balance decoding accuracy and computational cost.
result: The beam search decoder achieves high decoding accuracy while meeting latency requirements for real-time operation, avoiding the need for massive classical computation resources.
conclusion: The proposed decoder offers a promising approach for practical quantum error correction, enabling faster and more efficient decoding of quantum LDPC codes.

title: Planar Fault-Tolerant Circuits For Non-Clifford Gates On The 2d Color Code

Author(s): Andreas Bauer and Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente

A family of scalable circuits designed for universal quantum computing on planar chips with nearest-neighbor couplings called twisted color circuits is introduced and can achieve fault tolerance with a “just-in-time” decoder.

tldr: Introduces planar fault-tolerant circuits for non-Clifford gates on the 2D color code using twisted color circuits and a just-in-time decoder.
motivation: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computing on planar chips with nearest-neighbor couplings requires efficient non-Clifford gate implementations.
method: Proposes twisted color circuits, a family of scalable circuits, and a just-in-time decoder to achieve fault tolerance.
result: Demonstrates a scalable approach for non-Clifford gates on the 2D color code with planar geometry.
conclusion: The work advances fault-tolerant quantum computing on planar architectures, but is primarily a quantum error correction and fault tolerance contribution.

title: Quantifying Robustness And Locality Of Majorana Bound States In Interacting Systems

tldr: This paper rigorously defines Majorana bound states in interacting quantum-dot systems and quantifies their robustness and locality for non-Abelian braiding.
motivation: Recent quantum-dot experiments suggest Majorana bound states may exist, but their protection and feasibility for topological quantum computing need rigorous characterization in interacting systems.
method: The authors develop theoretical criteria to quantify the robustness and locality of Majorana bound states in interacting systems, likely using numerical simulations and analytical models.
result: They provide a quantitative framework to assess how interactions affect the Majorana bound states' protection and their potential for non-Abelian braiding operations.
conclusion: The work establishes rigorous definitions and measures for Majorana bound states in interacting systems, guiding experimental efforts toward topological quantum computing.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols

abstract:

method: The method propagates errors through the circuit to the end, reducing the complexity of simulating logical magic state preparation protocols.
result: The proposed technique enables efficient classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for analyzing magic state preparation, which is important for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Abelian Multi-Cycle Codes For Single-Shot Error Correction

motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but existing codes often require many rounds of syndrome extraction. Single-shot error correction reduces this overhead.
method: The authors construct Abelian multi-cycle codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, and analyze their single-shot error correction properties using belief propagation and ordered statistics decoding.
result: The proposed codes achieve a pseudothreshold of approximately 1.1% with significantly shorter block lengths compared to previous single-shot codes.
conclusion: Abelian multi-cycle codes offer a promising approach to efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation with reduced syndrome extraction overhead.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: A transformer-based neural network decoder for bivariate bicycle codes achieves lower logical error rates and faster runtime than BP-OSD on small codes, but performance degrades on larger codes.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum LDPC codes, but machine learning decoders have not been demonstrated for circuit-level noise on such codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is trained to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, using syndrome measurements as input and predicting error corrections.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the model achieves logical error rates nearly 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster; on the [[288,12,18]] code, logical error rates are worse but speed advantage remains.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and controlling memory effects in stochastic systems is important for accelerating relaxation dynamics, which has implications for material processing and nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
method: The authors use optical birefringence to monitor orientational dynamics of nanoparticles under AC electric fields, and model the relaxation using the Smoluchowski equation with a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients due to polydispersity.
result: They observe nonmonotonic Kovacs relaxation in two-step protocols and show that sequentially suppressing the slowest relaxation mode reduces relaxation time significantly compared to standard protocols.
conclusion: Memory effects in polydisperse suspensions can be mitigated by tailored multi-step protocols, providing a strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.

title: Superconducting Spiral Inductors For Rf Reflectometry: Operation At Elevated Temperatures And Magnetic Fields
authors: Euan Parry, Murat Cubukcu, Patrick Reuvekamp, Manoj Stanley, Jonathan D. Fletcher, Alessandro Rossi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.00172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting spiral inductors are emerging as key components for radio-frequency (RF) reflectometry, a widely used readout technique for semiconductor spin qubits. Future scalable quantum-computing architectures are expected to operate at elevated temperatures and magnetic fields, placing new demands on the performance and stability of superconducting circuit elements. Here, we present a systematic study of NbTiN spiral inductors under temperatures of several kelvin and magnetic fields approaching 1 T. By combining weakly coupled resonator measurements with independent two-port inductance extraction, we separate inductive and capacitive contributions to device behaviour and directly identify the origin of resonance shifts and quality factor degradation. Furthermore, we establish practical design metrics linking geometry, temperature sensitivity, and magnetic-field robustness. These results provide a general framework for benchmarking superconducting inductors and guiding the design of future RF-reflectometry circuits for practical quantum technologies.
tldr: This paper studies NbTiN superconducting spiral inductors for RF reflectometry readout of spin qubits, focusing on performance at elevated temperatures and magnetic fields.
motivation: Scalable quantum computing architectures require RF reflectometry components that operate reliably at higher temperatures and magnetic fields, but the performance of superconducting inductors under these conditions is not well understood.
method: The authors combine weakly coupled resonator measurements with independent two-port inductance extraction to separate inductive and capacitive contributions, and establish design metrics linking geometry, temperature sensitivity, and magnetic-field robustness.
result: They identify the origin of resonance shifts and quality factor degradation, and provide a framework for benchmarking superconducting inductors under realistic operating conditions.
conclusion: The results guide the design of future RF-reflectometry circuits for practical quantum technologies, but the work is primarily an engineering characterization without novel quantum information or thermodynamics insights.

title: Phase-space Open-system Dynamics Of Second-order Nonlinear Interactions With Pulsed Quantum Light
authors: Emanuel Hubenschmid And Victor Rueskov Christiansen
abstract:
Author(s): Emanuel Hubenschmid and Victor Rueskov Christiansen

The theoretical description of broadband, multimode quantum pulses undergoing a second-order [MATH]-nonlinear interaction can be quite intricate due to the large dimensionality of the underlying phase space. However, in many cases only a few broadband (temporal) modes are relevant before and af…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 063734] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a phase-space method to simulate open-system dynamics of broadband quantum pulses undergoing second-order nonlinear interactions.
motivation: Theoretical description of broadband multimode quantum pulses in nonlinear media is complex due to large phase-space dimensionality; a tractable method is needed.
method: The authors derive a phase-space representation using the Wigner function and model the open-system dynamics via a master equation, accounting for loss and noise.
result: They demonstrate that only a few temporal modes are relevant, enabling efficient simulation of the nonlinear interaction with pulsed quantum light.
conclusion: The phase-space approach provides a practical tool for analyzing quantum optical systems with second-order nonlinearities, but the work is primarily a computational technique without direct information-theoretic or thermodynamic implications.

title: Accelerated Spin-adapted Ground-state Preparation With Nonvariational Quantum Algorithms

motivation: Preparing ground states with specific total spin is important for quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics, but existing methods are often variational and slow.
method: The authors propose a nonvariational approach that incorporates penalty terms to enforce spin constraints and uses acceleration techniques to improve convergence.
result: The algorithm achieves faster preparation of spin-adapted ground states compared to variational methods, with demonstrated numerical examples.
conclusion: Nonvariational methods with penalty terms offer an efficient alternative for spin-constrained ground-state preparation on quantum computers.

motivation: Exceptional points in open quantum systems are of interest for non-Hermitian physics, but the paper's focus on spectral degeneracies in quadratic fermionic Liouvillians is not directly aligned with the researcher's core interests in quantum thermodynamics or information theory.
method: The authors use the third quantization formalism to analytically characterize higher-order exceptional points in quadratic Liouvillians.
result: They demonstrate the existence and properties of higher-order exceptional points in a general class of open fermionic models.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding exceptional points in dissipative fermionic systems, but its relevance to information thermodynamics or quantum information is indirect.

tldr: Maps non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians to Markov chain Laplacians, linking non-Hermitian physics to classical stochastic processes.
motivation: Non-Hermitian many-body systems are hard to realize physically; a mapping to Markov chains could simplify analysis and enable experimental simulation.
method: Proposes a general formalism that maps non-Hermitian Hamiltonians to Laplacians of Markov chains, using wave-function interpretation as probability distributions.
result: Establishes a correspondence between non-Hermitian dynamics and classical Markov processes, potentially allowing experimental emulation with classical stochastic systems.
conclusion: The mapping provides a new perspective on non-Hermitian many-body physics but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics of information processing.

method: The authors analyze a model with Rep(Q8) non-invertible symmetry using both Hamiltonian and Floquet dynamics, studying the symmetry's role through correlation functions and entanglement measures.

tldr: This paper studies the effect of Abrikosov vortices on the transmission of superconducting coplanar resonators, observing equidistant resonance jumps.
motivation: Superconducting resonators are key components in quantum circuits, but their performance degrades in magnetic fields due to vortices. Understanding this degradation is important for practical applications.
method: The authors measure the transmission parameter of niobium quarter-wave resonators as a function of magnetic field and analyze the resonance frequency shifts caused by individual vortex entry.
result: They observe equidistant jumps in the resonance frequency, corresponding to the sequential entry of single vortices, and model the effect using a simple geometric picture.
conclusion: The work provides insight into vortex dynamics in superconducting resonators, which is relevant for improving the performance of quantum devices in magnetic fields.

motivation: Previous studies on PbTe quantum dots reported conflicting observations of charging energy; this work aims to clarify the conditions under which charging energy appears.
method: The authors fabricate PbTe nanowires with different cross-sectional areas to vary quantum dot size and measure the charging energy evolution via transport spectroscopy.
result: They find that charging energy is present for small dots but absent for large dots, with a crossover at a certain size threshold.
conclusion: The presence of charging energy in PbTe quantum dots depends on dot size, resolving the earlier ambiguity and providing guidance for device design.

method: The authors design a quantum circuit that implements the Hadamard test and controlled unitary operations to estimate the Jones polynomial at roots of unity. They execute the algorithm on a trapped-ion quantum processor, using error mitigation techniques to improve results.

conclusion: While the work demonstrates a proof-of-principle quantum algorithm for the Jones polynomial, it does not yet achieve a quantum advantage and is primarily a benchmark study. The contribution is more about algorithm implementation and hardware demonstration than advancing quantum information theory.
